prompt: What does `=SUMIFS(H2:H109, G2:G109, "Wholesale")` add up?
hint: Read it aloud: add this, where that is…

choices.text: The number of rows whose channel is Wholesale
choices.why: That is a count, which is COUNTIFS. SUMIFS adds the values of its first range.

choices.text: The Revenue of every row whose Channel is Wholesale
choices.why: Right: add H wherever G is Wholesale. On this data it is R$ 38,731.

choices.text: The Revenue of the first wholesale row, then stops
choices.why: SUMIFS reads every row of the ranges, from 2 to 109, and adds all that pass.

choices.text: All of column H, plus the rows of column G that say Wholesale
choices.why: Column G holds text; it is tested, never added.

prompt: What does `=SUMIFS(H2:H109, D2:D109, "SUL1K", G2:G109, "Wholesale")` return on your `Sales` sheet?
hint: Type it in J2. The revenue, in reais.

prompt: You meant to type `"Wholesale"` and typed `"Wholesal"`. The cell shows 0. What gives the mistake away?
hint: What must the three channel totals do?

choices.text: Excel shows #VALUE! beside the cell
choices.why: A condition nothing meets is not an error. The answer is an ordinary 0.

choices.text: A green triangle appears in the corner of the cell
choices.why: Nothing marks the cell; the formula is valid and its answer is 0.

choices.text: The channel totals stop adding up to =SUM(H2:H109)
choices.why: Right. The parts must add to the whole, and the 38,731 missing from them is the only symptom.

choices.text: Nothing: criteria ignore case and letters alike
choices.why: They ignore case, so online finds Online. A missing letter is a different word.

prompt: Why does the course write `SUMIFS` even when there is only one condition?
hint: Where does SUMIF put the range to add?

choices.text: SUMIF was removed from Microsoft 365 and survives only in old files
choices.why: It still exists and old sheets are full of it.

choices.text: SUMIF cannot read a range that sits on another sheet of the workbook
choices.why: It can; that is not the reason.

choices.text: SUMIF puts the range to add last
choices.why: Right, and one order is easier to keep than two. Carrying one order into the other puts a condition where a range belongs.

choices.text: SUMIFS is always faster
choices.why: Speed is not the argument; the argument order is.

prompt: Which of these answer the revenue from `Online` or `Shop` sales, on this data? Choose all that apply.
hint: The conditions inside one SUMIFS are joined by and.

choices.text: `=SUMIFS(H2:H109, G2:G109, "Online")+SUMIFS(H2:H109, G2:G109, "Shop")`
choices.why: Two totals added: 11,143 + 1,620 = 12,763.

choices.text: `=SUMIFS(H2:H109, G2:G109, "Online", G2:G109, "Shop")`
choices.why: Both conditions must hold on one row, and no cell is both Online and Shop, so it answers 0.

choices.text: `=SUMIFS(H2:H109, G2:G109, "<>Wholesale")`
choices.why: While these are the only three channels, not Wholesale is Online or Shop: 12,763.

choices.text: `=SUMIFS(H2:H109, G2:G109, "Online or Shop")`
choices.why: The condition is compared with each cell as text, and no cell says Online or Shop.

prompt: `=COUNTIFS(G2:G109, "Online")` answers 47. What is 47?
hint: What does COUNTIFS count?

choices.text: The bags sold online
choices.why: That is SUMIFS over Bags, and it is 149.

choices.text: The number of online sales, one per row that passed
choices.why: Right. Forty-seven rows, which hold 149 bags between them.

choices.text: The number of different customers who bought online
choices.why: A customer with several online sales is several rows; COUNTIFS cannot count distinct customers.

choices.text: The online revenue in hundreds of reais
choices.why: COUNTIFS never looks at what is in Revenue; it counts rows.

prompt: How many wholesale sales were of ten bags or more? Use `COUNTIFS` on your `Sales` sheet.
hint: Two pairs: the channel, and the bags compared with 10.

prompt: Why can `COUNTIFS` not tell you how many different customers bought online?
hint: What happens to a customer who bought six times?

choices.text: Each sale is a row, so one customer counts once for every sale they made
choices.why: Right. Counting distinct values needs another tool; lesson 16 has one.

choices.text: The Customer column holds text and COUNTIFS counts only numbers
choices.why: COUNTIFS counts rows whatever they hold; it is COUNT that counts numbers.

choices.text: It needs the sheet sorted by customer first
choices.why: Sorting changes nothing about what COUNTIFS counts.

choices.text: The customers live on another sheet, which it cannot read
choices.why: The Customer codes are on Sales, and COUNTIFS reads other sheets anyway.

prompt: However many bags a sale holds, `COUNTIFS` adds one for it: the function counts ___, never what is in them.
hint: What one sale is on the Sales sheet.

prompt: `=AVERAGEIFS(E2:E109, D2:D109, "CER1K", G2:G109, "Shop")` answers `#DIV/0!`. What does it tell you?
hint: What does an average divide by?

choices.text: The average number of bags in that group is exactly zero
choices.why: An average of zero needs rows to average. Here there are none.

choices.text: The two test ranges are of different sizes and cannot be paired
choices.why: They are the same size; a mismatch gives #VALUE!.

choices.text: No sale passes both tests, so it divides by zero
choices.why: Right. Café Serra has never sold CER1K over the counter, and the error says the group is empty.

choices.text: The Bags column holds a number stored as text
choices.why: Text in Bags would be skipped, not turned into a division by zero.

prompt: Café Serra forecasts 300 bags of `CER1K` next half-year and wants the revenue. Which price per bag should multiply the 300?
hint: Which of the two averages multiplies back to the revenue it came from?

choices.text: R$ 110.11, the AVERAGEIFS of the Price column
choices.why: It counts each sale once, whatever its size, so 110.11 × 200 bags is not the R$ 21,356 that 200 bags brought in.

choices.text: R$ 118, today's list price
choices.why: Wholesale customers pay less than list, and most CER1K bags go to them.

choices.text: R$ 106.78, revenue divided by bags
choices.why: Right. It is weighted by bags, so it multiplies back: 106.78 × 200 is the R$ 21,356.

choices.text: The midpoint of 106.78 and 110.11
choices.why: Averaging two averages gives a number neither question asked for.

prompt: What is the average number of bags per sale over all 108 sales? Give it to two decimal places.
hint: AVERAGE over the Bags column, or the bags divided by the sales.

prompt: The channel averages of bags per sale are 10.6, 3.17 and 1.70. Their plain average is about 5.16, yet `=AVERAGE(E2:E109)` gives 5.47. Why?
hint: How many sales does each channel have?

choices.text: AVERAGE rounds each value to two decimals before it divides
choices.why: Nothing was rounded; both numbers are exact averages of different things.

choices.text: The channels have different numbers of sales
choices.why: Right, and the plain average gave them the same weight. 38, 47 and 23 sales are not equal groups, so only the totals divided once give the real average.

choices.text: AVERAGEIFS leaves out some rows that AVERAGE includes
choices.why: Between them the three channels cover all 108 rows.

choices.text: One of the three averages hides a #DIV/0! inside it
choices.why: All three groups have sales, so none divides by zero.

prompt: `=SUMIFS(H2:H109, B2:B109, ">=J1")` answers 0, though J1 holds 2026-01-01. Why?
hint: What is J1 when it sits inside the quotes?

choices.text: Inside the quotes, J1 is two characters of text, not a reference
choices.why: Right. Write ">="&J1: the operator in quotes, the reference outside, joined with &.

choices.text: Dates cannot be used as conditions
choices.why: They can; a date is a number, and a condition compares numbers.

choices.text: J1 must be formatted as text first
choices.why: It must stay a date. The problem is that the formula never reads it.

choices.text: SUMIFS needs a second condition to end the period
choices.why: One condition is allowed; it would give all of 2026 so far.

prompt: Why does the lesson end a year with `"<"&DATE(2026,1,1)` rather than `"<="&DATE(2025,12,31)`?
hint: Think of a value that carries a time of day.

choices.text: SUMIFS does not accept the <= operator
choices.why: It accepts <=; the problem is what <= leaves out.

choices.text: 31 December at 15:00 is larger than 31 December, and <= would leave it out
choices.why: Right. Ending at the next period's start is right with or without times, and needs no month lengths.

choices.text: DATE refuses the 31st of a month
choices.why: DATE(2025,12,31) is a perfectly good date.

choices.text: The two give different totals on this data
choices.why: On this data they agree, because the dates carry no time. The rule is for the data that does.

prompt: Match each condition to the cells that pass it.
hint: The table at the top of the section.

pairs.right: Anything except Wholesale, an empty cell included

prompt: How many bags of 1 kg were sold? Use a wildcard on the `Product` column.
hint: The 1 kg codes end in 1K.

prompt: A colleague reports retail revenue as `=SUMIFS(H2:H109, G2:G109, "<>Wholesale")`. Next year Café Serra starts selling at a weekly market, channel `Market`. What happens to the report?
hint: What does a not condition let in?

choices.text: It returns #VALUE! until the formula is updated
choices.why: A new value in the column is just another cell that passes or fails.

choices.text: Market sales are left out, because conditions match exact words
choices.why: The condition is not Wholesale, and Market is not Wholesale, so it passes.

choices.text: Excel asks which channels to include when the sheet is opened
choices.why: A formula asks nobody anything; it recalculates.

choices.text: The new channel passes the test and is added without a word
choices.why: Right. A not condition holds only while you know every value the column can take.

prompt: In the grid's formula, why is the product written `$A3` rather than `A3`?
hint: Fill the formula one column to the right and read where it points.

choices.text: Without the $, Excel refuses to fill the formula to the right
choices.why: Excel fills it happily; the cells just ask the wrong question.

choices.text: Filled right, A3 would become B3, which holds a count of bags
choices.why: Right, and the cell would find nothing. The $ keeps every column of the grid on column A, where the codes are.

choices.text: The $ makes the comparison ignore capitals
choices.why: Criteria ignore case already; $ is about which cell is read.

choices.text: $A3 stops the row moving when the formula is filled down
choices.why: That is A$3. $A3 lets the row move, so each row of the grid reads its own product.

prompt: Put the building of the Report grid in order.
hint: The labels first, then one formula, then the check.
items: Type the six product codes in A3 to A8
Type the first day of each month in B2 to D2
Fill it right to D3 and down to row 8
Add the totals and compare E9 with a single SUMIFS
trap: Typing the formula before the codes and dates exist gives zeros, which look exactly like months with no sales.

prompt: The grid shows the first quarter of 2025. What do you change to make it show the first quarter of 2026?
hint: Where does the grid's question live?

choices.text: The DATE inside every one of the eighteen formulas
choices.why: The formulas hold no date; they read B$2, C$2 and D$2.

choices.text: The three dates in B2, C2 and D2, and nothing else
choices.why: Right. Every cell recalculates, and E9 answers 117.

choices.text: The ranges, so they start at the first sale of 2026
choices.why: The ranges cover all 108 sales; the dates in the header pick the months.

choices.text: A copy of the sheet, with the Sales rows of 2026 pasted in
choices.why: No copy is needed. That is the point of a grid built from the records.

prompt: What was the wholesale revenue from 1 January 2026 to the end of the data? Write one `SUMIFS` on your `Sales` sheet.
hint: One condition on the channel, one on the date.

prompt: Wholesale revenue was R$ 27,603 in 2025 and R$ 11,128 in 2026. A slide says wholesale fell 60%. What is wrong with it?
hint: How many months does each number cover?

choices.text: Nothing: 11,128 is about 40% of 27,603, so it fell 60%
choices.why: The arithmetic is right and the comparison is not: six months against twelve.

choices.text: It should have used AVERAGEIFS rather than SUMIFS
choices.why: An average per sale answers a different question; the fault is the periods.

choices.text: 2026 covers six months and 2025 covers twelve
choices.why: Right: compare January to June with January to June. Put the two half-years in cells, as in section 05, and compare like with like.

choices.text: SUMIFS cannot compare two different years in one sheet
choices.why: It compares any dates you give it; the slide gave it unequal periods.

prompt: A student's grid total is 98 where the single SUMIFS over the quarter gives 116. Every cell holds a number. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: The single formula knows nothing about the grid.

choices.text: The single SUMIFS is wrong, because it ignores the products
choices.why: It does not need the products: all bags in the quarter is what the grid adds up to.

choices.text: A reference moved when it should have stayed
choices.why: Right, so some cells ask the wrong question. A missing $ still fills the grid with numbers; only the check shows that some are wrong.

choices.text: Excel rounds every SUMIFS in a grid
choices.why: These are counts of bags; nothing is rounded.

choices.text: The grid needs subtotals under each size before it can match
choices.why: Subtotals inside a grid are what lesson 1 warns against; they would make it count twice.
